notes: Ruling slot 7 = FLN under Boumediene's Revolutionary Council. FFS kept in 18 as in MD (has popularity). Ex-French-army officers (les DAF) as pro-Western bloc in 0; Krim's MDRA in 1; UDMA/Ferhat Abbas milieu in 2; UGTA in 3; PAGS in 4; UNEA in 5; Arabo-Islamic 'asala' wing in 6; Clan d'Oujda in 13; Sonatrach technocrats in 15. No Algerian Shia: slots 8/9 hold Mzab Ibadis (Bayyud's al-Hayat institute, the azzaba councils). Ba'athist teacher cells in 21 with the MD Ba'ath sprite.

0.name: Les DAF
0.english: The Deserters of the French Army
0.text:
Les DAF are the Algerian officers who served in the French army and crossed over to the liberation army late in the war. Under Boumediene they have become the professional backbone of the Ministry of National Defence, led by its secretary-general Abdelkader Chabou, and are resented by maquis veterans as opportunists.

French-trained and francophone, they favour a disciplined, modern army, technical competence over revolutionary credentials and pragmatic ties with France and the West in training and equipment. They are hostile to political commissars and to the guerrilla culture of the wilayas. Their leverage lies in staff positions, logistics and control over the army's modernization.

1.name: Mouvement démocratique pour le renouveau algérien
1.native_full: Mouvement démocratique pour le renouveau algérien
1.text:
The Democratic Movement for Algerian Renewal was founded in exile in 1967 by Krim Belkacem, a historic leader of the 1954 uprising and signatory of the Evian Accords. Sentenced to death in absentia in 1969, Krim directs the movement from Europe, gathering disillusioned veterans, Kabyle notables and émigré professionals.

The MDRA denounces Boumediene's military dictatorship and calls for political pluralism, civil liberties, an elected assembly and an economy open to private initiative. It seeks sympathy in France and the West without becoming their instrument. Its leverage lies in Krim's historic prestige, contacts in Kabylia and among émigrés, and the security services' fear of a conspiracy.

2.name: Union démocratique du manifeste algérien
2.english: Democratic Union of the Algerian Manifesto
2.text:
The Democratic Union of the Algerian Manifesto was Ferhat Abbas's moderate nationalist party of pharmacists, lawyers and teachers, dissolved in 1956 when its members joined the FLN. Abbas became the first president of the provisional government and of the Constituent Assembly, resigned in protest in 1963 and now lives in retirement in Algiers after house arrest.

Its liberal milieu wants constitutional government, a free press, independent courts and respect for private property and the professions. It favours a measured relationship with France and the West, though it remains committed to independence. Its leverage is moral rather than organizational: respected names among the francophone bourgeoisie of Algiers, Constantine and Sétif.
2.wiki: Democratic Union of the Algerian Manifesto

3.name: Union générale des travailleurs algériens
3.text:
The General Union of Algerian Workers was founded in 1956 by Aïssat Idir, who died in French custody, and joined the war of independence. After 1962 its leaders defended self-management and union autonomy, but successive congresses brought it under the control of the FLN apparatus, and by 1970 it is formally a mass organization of the party.

Within it, a current of autonomist unionists still argues for genuine collective bargaining, workers' councils in self-managed enterprises and wages that keep pace with industrialization. They favour social reform within a mixed state economy rather than Soviet-style planning. The union's leverage is its membership in the ports, railways, oil installations and new state industries.

4.name: Parti de l'avant-garde socialiste
4.text:
The Socialist Vanguard Party was founded clandestinely in January 1966 by former members of the Algerian Communist Party and left-wing FLN militants who had opposed Boumediene's coup. Led by Sadek Hadjerès and Bachir Hadj Ali, who was arrested and tortured in 1965, it remains illegal and works underground.

The PAGS follows Moscow's line, defends self-management and land reform and calls for the nationalization of oil and foreign interests. It offers critical support to any anti-imperialist measures by the regime while demanding democratic rights for workers. Its strength lies among unionists, teachers, students and intellectuals, and in the goodwill of the Soviet bloc.

5.name: Union nationale des étudiants algériens
5.text:
The National Union of Algerian Students is the heir of the wartime student union that called the 1956 strike for independence. After the 1965 coup it slipped from FLN control, became a stronghold of the clandestine left and led strikes in 1968 that brought police onto the campus of the University of Algiers.

Its militants demand university autonomy, democratic freedoms, radical agrarian reform and a socialism run from below rather than by colonels and bureaucrats. They admire Vietnam and the Palestinian resistance and distrust the regime's technocrats. Their leverage is the ability to paralyse the universities and to train the next generation of the Algerian left.

6.name: Ahl al-Asala
6.text:
The People of Authenticity are the Arabo-Islamic conservative wing of the regime, gathered around Education Minister Ahmed Taleb Ibrahimi, son of the reformist scholar Bachir Ibrahimi, and around Mouloud Kassim Naït Belkacem and the organizers of the seminars on Islamic thought. They rose inside the FLN and the ministries after the 1965 coup.

They demand rapid Arabization of schools and administration, the restoration of Islamic values, austere public morals and the uprooting of French cultural influence. Hostile to the West and to secular francophone elites, they accept state socialism if it wears an Islamic face. Their leverage lies in the education system, mosques and Arabic-speaking cadres of the party.

7.name: Jabhat al-Tahrir al-Watani
7.text:
The National Liberation Front launched the war of independence on 1 November 1954 and has been Algeria's single party since 1962. Since the coup of 19 June 1965 real power lies with the Revolutionary Council chaired by Colonel Houari Boumediene, while the party apparatus, headed by Kaid Ahmed since 1967, mobilizes and supervises the mass organizations.

The regime pursues state-led industrialization, control of hydrocarbons, Arabization and a planned socialist economy, while championing the Third World, the Palestinian cause and liberation movements. It is non-aligned but buys Soviet arms and confronts French oil companies. Its leverage rests on the army, the security services and the legitimacy of the liberation war.

8.name: Ma'had al-Hayat
8.text:
The Al-Hayat Institute in Guerrara was founded in 1925 by Shaykh Ibrahim Bayyud, the leading reformist scholar of the Ibadi community of the Mzab. Bayyud joined the Association of Muslim Ulama, supported independence and sat in the first national assembly; in 1970 his school is the intellectual centre of Algeria's only non-Sunni Muslim community.

The reformists combine Ibadi orthodoxy with modern Arabic education, scientific subjects and civic participation, and seek tolerance from the state in return for loyalty. They oppose atheism and moral laxity but avoid confrontation. Their leverage lies in the cohesive Mzabite merchant community, whose shops and commercial houses stretch from Ghardaïa to Algiers and Oran.

9.name: Halqat al-Azzaba
9.text:
The Council of the Azzaba is the ancient body of Ibadi clerics that governs religious and social life in the towns of the Mzab valley. Its members, chosen for learning and piety, still regulate marriage, morals, mosque property and community discipline, and can impose social exclusion on those who defy them.

The azzaba hold that the community must be ruled by its religious scholars and defend strict observance, the separation of the Mzab from outside influences and the authority of clerical courts. They resist both state secularization and the reformers of Guerrara. Their power lies in the mosques of Ghardaïa, Beni Isguen and Melika and in communal solidarity.

10.name: Al-Tariqa al-Tijaniyya
10.text:
The Tijaniyyah is the Sufi brotherhood founded by Ahmad al-Tijani at Ain Madhi in the late eighteenth century, with its mother lodges at Ain Madhi and Temacine and millions of followers across West Africa. Stigmatized by nationalists for its accommodation with colonial France, it survives in Algeria under official suspicion.

Its shaykhs preach quietist piety, obedience to legitimate authority, veneration of saints and the social role of the zawiyas in charity and education. They seek state recognition and protection of their lands and pilgrimages. Their leverage lies in rural devotion in the south and in prestige among foreign disciples that Algerian diplomacy in Africa could use.

11.name: Shuyukh al-Rafd
11.text:
The Sheikhs of Refusal are the radical preachers who emerged from the old Association of Muslim Ulama, above all Abdellatif Soltani and Ahmed Sahnoun, who denounce the regime's socialism as godless. Without organization or legal platform, they speak from private mosques and circulate sermons among students and pious merchants.

They reject secular nationalism, Soviet friendship and Western culture alike and call for a state governed wholly by Islamic law as part of a wider Muslim community. Their followers see the coming land reform and the emancipation of women as attacks on religion. Their leverage is moral authority over a young generation searching for an Islamic alternative.

12.name: Al-Qiyam al-Islamiyya
12.text:
Al-Qiyam, the Association of Islamic Values, was founded in 1963 by Hachemi Tidjani and drew on the ideas of the thinker Malek Bennabi and the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood. It campaigned against alcohol, Western morals and the secular left, and protested the execution of Sayyid Qutb in 1966, after which the authorities restricted its activities.

The association calls for an Islamic state, the application of the sharia, Arabic education and the defence of the family against socialist secularism. It is hostile to both communism and Western cultural influence. Though weakened, it has seeded a network of mosque circles and student activists that the regime cannot easily suppress.

13.name: Le Clan d'Oujda
13.text:
The Oujda Clan is the inner circle that formed around Boumediene in the general staff of the frontier army based in Oujda during the war. It includes Foreign Minister Abdelaziz Bouteflika, Interior Minister Ahmed Medeghri, Cherif Belkacem and Kaid Ahmed, and dominates the state that emerged from the 1965 coup.

Its members prize order, centralized administration, pragmatic diplomacy and a strong state above parties and ideology. They balance between Moscow and the West to secure Algeria's interests and treat the FLN as an instrument rather than a master. Their leverage is control of key ministries, the prefectures and the personal trust of the president.

14.name: Jam'iyyat al-Ulama al-Muslimin al-Jaza'iriyyin
14.text:
The Association of Algerian Muslim Ulema was founded in 1931 by Abdelhamid Ben Badis to revive Islam and the Arabic language against colonial assimilation. It joined the FLN during the war and was not permitted to reconstitute itself after independence; its president Bachir Ibrahimi died in 1965 after criticizing Ben Bella's regime.

Its former members, teachers and graduates of its free schools stand for Islamic reform, Arabic education, moral conservatism and the motto that Islam is our religion, Arabic our language and Algeria our homeland. They are neither pro-Soviet nor pro-Western. Their influence runs through the school system, mosques and the conservative provincial towns of the east.

15.name: Sonatrach
15.native_full: Société nationale pour la recherche, la production, le transport, la transformation et la commercialisation des hydrocarbures
15.text:
Sonatrach, the national hydrocarbons company created in 1963, has become the heart of the Algerian economy under its director-general Sid Ahmed Ghozali and Industry and Energy Minister Belaid Abdesselam. It is steadily taking over pipelines, refineries and distribution and prepares to challenge the French concessions guaranteed after independence.

Its managers form a new industrial elite committed to the strategy of industrializing industries: oil and gas revenues financing steelworks, petrochemicals and heavy industry. They are pragmatic nationalists who trade with American firms while confronting French companies. Their leverage is control of the country's foreign exchange and the patronage of the industrial investment programme.

16.name: Union générale des commerçants algériens
16.text:
The General Union of Algerian Merchants was founded in 1956 by the FLN to organize Muslim shopkeepers and traders behind the independence struggle. Since independence it has represented the small commerce, craftsmen and private businesses that survive alongside the state sector, formally as a mass organization of the party.

Its members want freedom to trade, fair access to import licences and supplies, low taxation and protection from the expansion of state monopolies and cooperatives. They fear the coming agrarian revolution and nationalizations. Their leverage lies in the distribution of everyday goods, the informal economy and the family networks of the merchant towns.

17.name: Les Reboiseurs
17.text:
The Reforesters are the foresters, agronomists and engineers of the forestry administration and the National Agronomic Institute at El Harrach who warn that erosion, overgrazing and the destruction of forests during the war are pushing the Sahara northward. They have no organization beyond professional circles and ministerial committees.

They call for a great green belt of trees across the steppe, soil conservation, restoration of the cedar and cork oak forests and careful use of water in the High Plateaus. Indifferent to the Cold War, they seek to harness national service and state planning for ecological ends. Their leverage is technical expertise the regime increasingly values.

18.name: Front des forces socialistes
18.text:
The Socialist Forces Front was founded in September 1963 by Hocine Aït Ahmed, one of the historic leaders of the revolution, and led an armed revolt in Kabylia against Ben Bella. Captured and sentenced to death, Aït Ahmed escaped from El Harrach prison in 1966 and now leads the clandestine party from exile in Switzerland.

The FFS stands for a pluralist democratic socialism, civil liberties, a constituent assembly and respect for Algeria's Berber identity. It is non-aligned and rejects military rule and the single party. Its leverage lies in Kabylia, among émigré workers in France and in Aït Ahmed's revolutionary legitimacy.

19.name: Parti de la révolution socialiste
19.text:
The Party of the Socialist Revolution was founded in September 1962 by Mohamed Boudiaf, the coordinator of the 1954 uprising, in opposition to Ben Bella's seizure of power. Banned, its leader imprisoned and then exiled, the PRS has survived as a small clandestine organization led by Boudiaf from abroad.

It calls for a socialist revolution led by workers and peasants rather than by the army, independent of both Moscow and Beijing, together with democratic freedoms and the end of the single party. It denounces Boumediene's regime as state capitalism. Its leverage is limited to émigré militants in France and the prestige of a founding father of the revolution.

20.name: Organisation nationale des moudjahidine
20.text:
The National Organization of Mujahideen is the veterans' association of the war of independence, grouping former fighters of the liberation army and the civilian organization of the FLN. Officially a mass organization of the party, it administers pensions, licences and privileges granted to those with a proven record in the struggle.

Its members see themselves as the true guardians of the revolution, demand jobs, land and respect for veterans and resent technocrats and latecomers who now hold power. Fiercely nationalist and anti-French, they use populist rhetoric about betrayal and corruption. Their leverage is moral authority, local networks in every village and influence among officers who fought in the maquis.

21.name: Khalaya al-Ba'th
21.text:
The Ba'ath Cells are small clandestine circles of Algerian students returned from Damascus and Baghdad and of the Syrian and Iraqi teachers recruited by the thousands to Arabize the schools. Illegal under the single-party state, they meet in teachers' lodgings and student residences and keep contacts with both rival Ba'ath leaderships.

They demand total Arabization, the unity of the Arab nation from the Atlantic to the Gulf, a vanguard party and war against Zionism and Western imperialism. They despise francophone elites and Berberist claims. Their leverage is limited, but they shape the outlook of young Arabic-speaking teachers spreading through the education system.

22.name: Al-Jaysh al-Watani al-Sha'bi
22.text:
The People's National Army is the successor of the National Liberation Army of the war and the true foundation of the Boumediene regime. Equipped with Soviet arms and trained with Soviet and Egyptian help, it crushed the attempted coup of chief of staff Colonel Tahar Zbiri in December 1967; Zbiri has fled abroad.

The army sees itself as guardian of the revolution and of national unity, above parties and civilian politicians. Its officers favour a strong centralized state, heavy industry, national service and an independent foreign policy. Rivalries between maquis veterans and French-trained officers divide it, but its regional commands remain the decisive force in Algerian politics.

23.name: Dar al-Amir
23.text:
The House of the Emir is the family of Emir Abdelkader, who led the resistance against French conquest from 1832 to 1847 and ruled an Islamic state in western Algeria. His descendants, settled in Damascus since his exile, are honoured by the republic, which brought the emir's remains home in 1966.

A few conservative notables and religious families in Mascara and the west dream of a Muslim monarchy under the emir's line, combining Islamic legitimacy with national unity and free of party rule. They have no organization and little hope, but the emir's prestige is so central to national memory that any appeal in his name carries weight.
